options: Before the forward pass, using the counts the forward pass will produce
Inside the loss, so autograd can adjust it
After `opt.step()`, under `torch.no_grad()`, using the counts recorded by this step's forward pass, and before an evaluation pass overwrites them
Only at the end of training, once
explain: Algorithm 1 adjusts the bias from the load just observed, outside the gradient computation. Running it inside autograd would make it a learned parameter (and leak balance into the loss), and running it after an eval forward would balance the wrong batch. Counts from the current step only steer the next step's routing, so no future token leaks.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Secure Boot keys: PK, KEK, db and dbx
question: An attacker obtains the private key of one KEK enrolled on a fleet of laptops, but not the PK. What can they do?
options: Nothing, only the PK matters
Replace the PK
Sign db and dbx updates, for example adding their own certificate to db
Read the TPM's private keys
explain: Per the UEFI spec, db and dbx updates must be signed by a KEK or the PK. A KEK holder can therefore add an allowed certificate. Replacing the PK needs the PK private key.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: The 2023 to 2026 Microsoft certificate rollover
question: Why did Microsoft add the PCA 2011 certificate to dbx instead of continuing to add hashes of vulnerable boot managers?
options: Listing every vulnerable boot manager by hash was unreliable and costly; revoking the CA distrusts all of them at once
Hashes cannot be stored in dbx
The certificate had already expired
To free space in db
explain: Hash revocation misses rebuilds and consumes dbx space. Distrusting the signing certificate catches every boot manager it signed, at the cost of requiring a newly signed boot manager and updated media.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Hardware roots of trust: Boot Guard, AMD PSB and Apple silicon
question: A data-centre team buys used servers whose AMD CPUs were fused for another vendor's firmware key with PSB. What should they expect?
options: The CPUs will only boot firmware signed with that vendor's key, because PSB fuses cannot be undone
The CPUs reset to factory state on first boot
PSB turns itself off
Only Secure Boot is affected
explain: Cloudflare notes there is no way to roll a fused CPU back to unfused. PSB binds the processor to the OEM's firmware signing key, which is the security property and also the resale catch.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: A defender's firmware playbook, and where to practise
question: A Windows laptop shows a new PCR4 boot application in its measured boot log, PCR7 unchanged, and Defender reported as stopped. Which layer do you examine first?
options: The SPI flash, because PCR7 is unchanged
Only the network
Nothing, PCR7 is fine so Secure Boot passed
The ESP boot files, because a new boot application in PCR4 points to a changed boot chain
explain: PCR4 records boot applications; a new one means something new ran from the ESP. An unchanged PCR7 only says the Secure Boot variables and the signing authorities used look the same; trusted-but-old binaries, as in BlackLotus, can run without changing them (a new signer, such as the third-party CA behind shim, would show up there).

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-3 inside a warpgroup, and FP8 done accurately
question: Why does multiplying both Q and K by a random orthogonal matrix reduce FP8 error without changing the attention output?
options: It shrinks every value toward zero, so rounding errors are smaller
Scores are preserved because $MM^\top = I$, and mixing entries spreads outliers so one scale fits all entries better
It sorts the head dimension so outliers end up in a single block that is kept in FP16
It converts the values to integers, which FP8 represents exactly
explain: Orthogonality keeps $QK^\top$ identical. Each rotated entry is a signed sum of many original entries, which evens out magnitudes (max/RMS fell from 1.99 to 1.07 in the toy example), so quantization with a shared scale loses less information.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: Using and measuring the kernels: benchmarks, numerics, decoding
question: A decode step has 16 tiles (batch 1, 16 heads, one query row each) and a 32K-token KV cache on a 132-SM GPU. What does split-KV change?
options: It drops the chunks with small log-sum-exp, approximating attention
It reads fewer bytes of the KV cache
It spreads each head's keys over several thread blocks so many SMs read the cache at once, then merges the partial results exactly
It packs more query rows into each tile, so the same 16 thread blocks do more work
explain: Every key is still read once, plus a small partial output per chunk, and the log-sum-exp merge is exact, so nothing is approximated. The gain is parallelism: 16 thread blocks become 16 times the number of splits, loading the cache in parallel. Packing more query rows per tile is a different trick (used for grouped-query attention), not split-KV.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Load-balanced scheduling, plan and run, and CUDA graphs
question: Why does FlashInfer's split-KV reduction avoid atomic adds, unlike some Stream-K implementations?
options: Atomics are not available on Hopper
Atomic accumulation order varies between runs, so outputs would not be deterministic
Atomics would use too much workspace
LSE values cannot be added
explain: The paper says LLM serving requires deterministic outputs, so it dropped Stream-K's atomic aggregation. The plan fixes a reduction map, and the contraction kernel merges partial states in the same order every time the same lengths appear.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: The training target: straight lines and their velocity
question: Which statement about conditional flow matching is correct?
options: It needs the marginal velocity field computed over the whole dataset at every step
It only works with straight-line paths
Regressing onto per-sample conditional velocities gives the same gradient as regressing onto the intractable marginal velocity
It trains by maximizing the log-likelihood of the data under the ODE
explain: Lipman et al. Theorem 2: the CFM and FM losses differ by a constant independent of the parameters, so their gradients match. Straight OT paths are one choice; diffusion-style Gaussian paths also fit the framework.

courseTitle: Formal methods for security: protocol proofs and verified systems
lessonTitle: Three messages, seventeen years: Lowe's attack on Needham-Schroeder
question: In Lowe's attack, which cryptographic assumption does the intruder break?
options: It decrypts {Na, Nb} pk(A) without A's private key
None: every ciphertext is opened only by the holder of the matching private key
It guesses Nb by brute force
It forges A's signature on message 3
explain: The intruder only decrypts messages encrypted to its own key and forwards the rest. A does the critical decryption for it. Protocol-level attacks of this kind are invisible to anyone checking only the strength of the algorithms.

courseTitle: Formal methods for security: protocol proofs and verified systems
lessonTitle: ProVerif: protocols as processes, proofs by Horn clauses
question: ProVerif reports "RESULT ... cannot be proved" for a secrecy query and shows a derivation that you cannot turn into a real run. What should the report say?
options: The protocol is broken
The protocol is proven secure
Unknown: the tool's abstraction found a possible derivation but no attack; refine the model or try another tool
ProVerif crashed
explain: "Cannot be proved" is ProVerif's don't-know answer. The usual next steps are to inspect the derivation, adjust the model (for example where fresh values are generated) or cross-check with Tamarin.

courseTitle: Formal methods for security: protocol proofs and verified systems
lessonTitle: 5G AKA, Signal and MLS: analyses that changed standards
question: Cremers and Dehnel-Wild found a race condition in 5G-AKA that an operator could introduce while following the standard. Where was the root cause?
options: Unstated assumptions about the channels between network components
A weak cipher on the radio link
A bug in Tamarin
Users choosing weak PINs
explain: Their abstract: security "critically relies on unstated assumptions on the inner workings of the underlying channels". The specification allowed an insecure but conforming implementation; the fix was to make the requirement explicit.

courseTitle: Formal methods for security: protocol proofs and verified systems
lessonTitle: Automated reasoning at cloud scale: Zelkova, s2n and Cedar
question: A Zelkova-style check of "policy Y allows only students and TAs" returns unsat. What does that mean?
options: The solver ran out of time
Some request from another principal is allowed
The policy is syntactically invalid
No request from anyone else is allowed by Y, for every possible principal, action and resource
explain: The question is encoded as: find a request Y allows whose principal is neither students nor tas. Unsat means no such request exists, so the property holds for all requests, not only the ones someone thought to test.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Why tests miss bugs that hide in rare interleavings
question: Which bug is TLA+ with TLC best placed to find?
options: An off-by-one in a Rust parsing function
A slow SQL query
A replication protocol that loses committed data if a node crashes during a membership change
A typo in a configuration file
explain: TLA+ checks the design: every interleaving of protocol steps and failures in a small model. Code-level slips like an off-by-one in a Rust function are what Verus-style code proofs (or tests) target.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Modeling a distributed protocol: messages, loss and duplication
question: With WF_vars(Next) and a TMCrash action, Termination fails with r3 stuck in prepared. Which change makes Termination hold while keeping crashes in the model?
options: Let the TM recover with its durable state (tmPrepared survives the crash), or replace the single TM with a replicated coordinator
Add strong fairness on TMCommit
Remove the Consistent invariant
Switch msgs to FIFO sequences
explain: Nothing is enabled for r3 after a permanent crash, so no fairness condition can force progress. Progress needs the decision maker to come back or to be replicated, the idea behind Paxos Commit. TLC confirms the first fix for a TM that may crash once and then recovers: Termination holds over 640 states. FIFO channels change ordering, not the missing decision.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Connecting specs to running code, and the wider tool map
question: You maintain a Go service that implements a TLA+ spec of a leader-lease protocol. The spec passes TLC, but you suspect the code has drifted from it. What is the cheapest step that would detect drift?
options: Rewrite the service in Rust and verify it with Verus
Prove the spec with TLAPS
Log the service's protocol events in integration tests and check the traces against the spec with TLC
Increase the model size in TLC
explain: Drift is a code-versus-spec question. Trace validation answers it using tests you already run, as the etcd and CCF projects do. TLAPS and bigger models only say more about the spec; a Verus rewrite would work but costs far more.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: FP8 beyond the GEMM: communication, optimizer state, memory, speed
question: GEMMs take 60% of a BF16 training step. FP4 makes them 4x faster and nothing else changes. What is the best possible step speedup?
options: About 1.8x
4x
explain: 1 / ((1 - 0.6) + 0.6 / 4) = 1 / (0.4 + 0.15) = 1.82. The 40% that is not GEMM work now dominates the step. Casting overhead would lower it further.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Pretraining in NVFP4: the four-part recipe and its results
question: You apply stochastic rounding to every tensor, including forward-pass activations and weights. What does the NVFP4 report predict?
options: Better accuracy, since all bias is removed
Worse results: SR on forward tensors adds quantization noise; it pays off mainly on gradients, where bias accumulates
No change, because SR and nearest rounding have the same expected value
Training cannot start, since SR is undefined for weights
explain: SR trades bias for variance. For gradients, which are summed across many steps and microbatches, removing bias matters most. For forward tensors the extra noise simply makes each forward pass less accurate, which the report found harmful.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Credential stuffing at scale, and 23andMe's relatives
question: What made the 23andMe incident so much larger than 14,000 accounts?
options: The attacker cracked the password database
An API returned all users' data without authentication
A sharing feature let each taken account read data about many relatives
The attacker bribed an employee
explain: Per the company, about 14,000 accounts were accessed by credential stuffing, and through DNA Relatives and Family Tree they reached about 6.9 million profiles. Feature design set the blast radius.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: CAPTCHAs, their limits and privacy-preserving tokens
question: Your signup form shows a CAPTCHA, but bot signups did not fall at all. The browser sends `captcha_ok=1` after a successful solve. What is the most likely flaw?
options: The puzzle is too easy
Bots are using residential proxies
The CAPTCHA is not localised
The server trusts a client-set field instead of verifying a token with the challenge service
explain: Scripts never load the puzzle; they post `captcha_ok=1` directly. The server must verify a token server-side, as Stripe's guidance stresses. Easy puzzles or proxies would reduce effectiveness, not eliminate it entirely.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Card payments from zero: who is who, and where fraud lands
question: A stolen card number is used on your online shop. The issuer approved it. Two months later the real cardholder disputes it. Without 3-D Secure, who usually bears the loss?
options: The merchant
The issuer, because it approved the payment
The card network
The cardholder
explain: For card-not-present fraud the default rules put the loss on the merchant through the chargeback. Authentication such as 3-D Secure can shift that liability to the issuer (lesson 14).

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: From risk score to decision: rules, models, step-up and review
question: A new 3-D Secure flow loses 40% of good customers who face it. What happens to the range of scores where step-up is the best action?
options: It narrows, because each challenge now costs more in lost good orders
It widens
It is unchanged
Step-up becomes best everywhere
explain: The step-up cost term $(1-p)dG$ grows with d, so step-up beats allow only at higher p and beats block only at lower p. Measuring abandonment is part of measuring a control.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Adaptive adversaries: shadow mode, response and running the programme
question: A new rule looks great in a backtest. What is the safest way to launch it?
options: Turn it on for all traffic at once to stop fraud quickly
Launch it only on weekends
Run it in shadow mode to measure would-be hits against maturing labels, then enable it gradually
Announce the rule publicly as a deterrent
explain: Shadow mode measures false positives on live traffic without harming anyone; a gradual rollout limits damage if the backtest missed something.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: Trading latency for throughput: commit_delay and async commit
question: A server has a single active client and commit_delay = 2000 microseconds with commit_siblings = 0. What happens to that client?
options: Each commit gets about 2 ms slower and throughput drops, since nobody else can join
Nothing, since commit_delay is ignored with one client
Commits get faster because flushes are batched
Commits become asynchronous
explain: With commit_siblings = 0 the sibling check always passes, so the lone leader sleeps 2 ms before every flush with no one to share it. That is pure added latency. The default commit_siblings = 5 exists to skip the sleep when joiners are unlikely.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Coverage-guided fuzzing: how AFL's edge bitmap steers mutation
question: What does the shift in prev_location = cur_location >> 1 achieve?
options: It makes A then B land in a different slot from B then A, and keeps a block jumping to itself distinct
It halves the map size
It randomises block numbers at run time
It counts how many times each block ran
explain: Without the shift, A XOR B equals B XOR A, and A XOR A is zero for every block, so direction and tight loops would be lost. Shifting the previous location breaks that symmetry.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Seeds, dictionaries and corpus minimisation
question: What does libFuzzer's -merge=1 MIN corpus/ do?
options: Copies into MIN only the inputs from corpus/ that add coverage not already in MIN
Deletes crashing inputs from corpus/
Merges two fuzzers into one process
Minimises each input to its smallest size
explain: The docs: inputs from the second and later directories that trigger new coverage are merged into the first. It shrinks a corpus to a coverage-equivalent subset; per-input shrinking is a different feature (-minimize_crash or reduce_inputs).

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Fuzzing beyond C: Go, Rust, Python and property-based testing
question: What is the oracle in the Hypothesis example?
options: The property decode(encode(name)) == name, which must hold for every generated string
A crash or hang
AddressSanitizer
Code coverage
explain: Property-based testing finds wrong answers, not just crashes. The round-trip property caught a failure that raises nothing at all: the two-character string U+0080 then "0" decodes back as U+0080 alone, a silently wrong answer. The cause is that the length byte counts characters instead of bytes.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: AI-assisted vulnerability discovery: what is verified so far
question: Why did OSS-Fuzz's long-running SQLite fuzzing miss the bug Big Sleep found?
options: The OSS-Fuzz harness was not built with the generate_series extension, and AFL on the right binary did not find it in 150 CPU-hours
SQLite has no fuzz targets
The bug only occurs on Windows
Fuzzers cannot find stack bugs
explain: The Big Sleep post: the harness configuration left the extension out, and a dedicated AFL attempt with the needed keywords still failed. Reach and difficulty, not lack of fuzzing, explain the miss.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Transpositions and Indel: which edits count changes the answer
question: You are building a structure whose correctness depends on the triangle inequality (lesson 7). Which distance is unsafe to plug in?
options: Levenshtein
Indel
Optimal string alignment (OSA)
True Damerau-Levenshtein
explain: OSA violates the triangle inequality: CA to AC is 1, AC to ABC is 1, but CA to ABC is 3. A search structure that prunes with that inequality could skip a real match. Levenshtein, Indel and true Damerau-Levenshtein are metrics.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Levenshtein automata, SymSpell and fuzzy queries in production
question: With Elasticsearch `fuzziness: AUTO` (default 3,6), how many edits are allowed for the terms `ox`, `cat` and `kitchen`?
options: 2, 2 and 2
1, 1 and 2
0, 1 and 2
0, 1 and 1
explain: AUTO:3,6 means lengths 0 to 2 must match exactly, 3 to 5 allow one edit, and more than 5 allow two. `ox` has 2 characters (0 edits), `cat` 3 (1 edit), `kitchen` 7 (2 edits).

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Geometric hashing: basis pairs, a hash table, and votes
question: You switch from similarity transforms to full 2D affine transforms (adding shear and non-uniform scale). What changes in the scheme?
options: The basis needs three non-collinear points, so preprocessing grows from O(Mn^3) to O(Mn^4)
Nothing; two points still define the frame
Hashing no longer works and you must compare all models directly
You need a 3D hash table
explain: Affine maps have 6 degrees of freedom, so 3 points are needed to fix a frame (the overview lists a three-point basis for 2D affine). With c = 3 the preprocessing cost O(Mn^(c+1)) becomes O(Mn^4), and recognition must try ordered triples of scene points.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: From an accepted match to a WCS header, and the triangle alternative
question: A solved WCS has CD matrix entries giving sqrt(|det CD|) = 0.000556 degrees per pixel. What is the pixel scale in arcseconds?
options: 0.556 arcsec/px
33.4 arcsec/px
0.0333 arcsec/px
2.0 arcsec/px
explain: One degree is 3600 arcsec, so 0.000556 x 3600 = 2.0 arcsec per pixel. The square root of the determinant removes the rotation and leaves the linear scale.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Better cells on the sphere: S2 cubes and H3 hexagons
question: You aggregate ride pickups into cells and smooth each cell's count with its immediate neighbors. Why might you pick H3 over geohash here?
options: Every H3 cell's neighbors are all the same distance from it, so equal smoothing weights make sense
H3 cells all have exactly the same area at every resolution
H3 IDs sort so that every pair of neighbors has consecutive IDs
H3 has no pentagons, so every cell has 6 neighbors
explain: Hexagon neighbors are equidistant, unlike square cells, whose diagonal neighbors are farther than edge neighbors. H3 cell areas vary (up to about 2 times within a resolution), no ordering makes all neighbors consecutive, and every resolution has exactly 12 pentagons with 5 neighbors each.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Warp and affine: an inverse map plus a border rule
question: Why do warp kernels evaluate the inverse transform rather than the forward one?
options: Because the inverse matrix has fewer coefficients, so it costs fewer FMAs
Because a forward scatter writes conflicting pixels and leaves destination holes, while an inverse gather writes each output exactly once
Because only the inverse map can be combined with interpolation
Because the forward map needs atomics for correctness, and atomics are unavailable in image kernels
explain: The gather form gives every destination pixel exactly one owning thread: no write conflicts, no holes, coalesced stores. Rounding the 16 pixels of a 30 degree rotated 4x4 forward fills only 12 of its 16 output cells. The inverse matrix is the same size as the forward one, and interpolation works in either direction, so neither of the other reasons holds.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Why frameworks do not call cudaMalloc for every tensor
question: A script deletes its only large tensor and nvidia-smi still shows the same usage. What best explains this?
options: The tensor leaked because Python did not run its destructor
The caching allocator kept the freed block in its pool, so the memory is still reserved
cudaFree is asynchronous and will finish on the next kernel launch
nvidia-smi only refreshes once per training step
explain: With caching, a free returns the block to PyTorch's pool, not to the driver. memory_allocated() drops; memory_reserved() and nvidia-smi do not until empty_cache() or an OOM retry releases whole free segments.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Fixed-size suballocation for the KV cache, and diagnosing OOMs
question: Why does a pool of equal-size KV blocks have no external fragmentation?
options: Because blocks are always allocated at adjacent addresses
Because the GPU defragments memory in the background
Because any free block can satisfy any request for a block, so free memory is never too scattered to use
Because each request's maximum length is reserved up front
explain: External fragmentation means free memory exists but not in a usable shape. With one block size and a block table for indirection, any free block is usable by any request, so all free blocks count.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Shared memory banks and bank conflicts
question: You pad a tile to `__shared__ float t[32][34];` and a warp reads `t[threadIdx.x][5]`. What happens?
options: No conflict, because the tile is padded
A 2-way bank conflict
A 32-way bank conflict
A broadcast, because every thread uses column 5
explain: Thread i reads word 34i + 5, bank (2i + 5) mod 32. Only 16 banks are used, each by two different words, so the greatest common divisor of 34 and 32, which is 2, gives 2 passes. Odd widths like 33 avoid it.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Occupancy: what it buys and what caps it
question: Theoretical occupancy is 75 percent but achieved occupancy is 31 percent. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The launch configuration is wrong and should use smaller blocks
The register allocation granularity was not accounted for
Shared memory is the real limiter rather than registers
The work is unbalanced: blocks differ a lot in cost, or most SMs are idle during a long tail
explain: Theoretical occupancy is what the launch configuration allows; achieved occupancy is the time average the hardware reached. Nsight Compute's own Occupancy section says large discrepancies between theoretical and achieved occupancy typically indicate highly imbalanced workloads. Check waves per SM and the per-SM active-cycle spread before touching registers or block size.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Computing a thread's global index: vector add end to end
question: In a 2D launch with blockDim = (16, 16), which pair of threads in the same block are neighbors in the linear thread order?
options: threadIdx (3, 5) and (3, 6)
threadIdx (3, 5) and (5, 3)
No pair: 2D blocks have no linear order
threadIdx (3, 5) and (4, 5)
explain: x moves fastest. (3, 5) has linear id 3 + 5 x 16 = 83 and (4, 5) has 84. Moving one step in y jumps by blockDim.x = 16.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Why chunk retrieval cannot answer 'what are the main themes?'
question: Which question is the best fit for GraphRAG's global search rather than plain vector RAG?
options: What year was Quillfern Labs founded?
Across all 2,000 support tickets, what recurring complaint themes appear?
Which supplier makes the Rover X2 drive motors?
What is Ben Ortiz's job title?
explain: The ticket-themes question needs a summary over the whole corpus, with no single chunk similar to the query. The other three are local fact lookups that top-k retrieval answers well and more cheaply.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: What GraphRAG costs and how its gains were measured
question: A team reports "GraphRAG wins 80% of the time" using an LLM judge on comprehensiveness only. What is the best follow-up check, following the paper's design?
options: Nothing, 80% is decisive
Switch the judge to a smaller model
Remove the questions where GraphRAG lost
Also report a control criterion like directness, and validate with a judge-independent measure such as claim counts
explain: The paper adds directness as a control (vector RAG should win it, and does) and validates comprehensiveness and diversity with claim extraction. LLM judges have biases, so a sanity check matters.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Why PPO is costly for LLMs and what GRPO removes
question: Why is training a per-token critic especially awkward for LLM reasoning tasks?
options: Tokens are discrete, so value functions cannot be defined
Critics cannot be initialized from pretrained models
Value models require a larger vocabulary
The reward usually arrives only at the final token, so the critic must predict a distant outcome from every partial answer
explain: With an outcome reward at the end of a long chain of thought, the critic must predict from each prefix whether the final answer will be right, a hard regression problem. DeepSeekMath cites this as a motivation for GRPO.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Failure modes and fixes: dead groups, entropy collapse, length bias
question: Halfway through training, 60% of your prompts are solved by all 16 samples. What is the most direct fix?
options: Raise the KL coefficient
Filter out groups whose rewards are all equal and keep sampling until the batch has enough informative groups (dynamic sampling), or add harder prompts
Lower the learning rate
Divide advantages by the response length
explain: All-correct groups have zero advantage and contribute no gradient, so 60% of your rollouts are wasted. Dynamic sampling refills the batch with mixed-outcome groups; a harder curriculum attacks the cause.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: Service days, calendar exceptions and times past 24:00
question: A feed has WKDY in calendar.txt (Mon to Fri) and a row WKDY, 20260704, exception_type 1 for Saturday July 4. What happens on July 4?
options: Nothing, Saturdays are 0 in calendar.txt so the exception is ignored
The feed is invalid because the date is outside the weekly pattern
Only trips with times past 24:00:00 run
All WKDY trips run on July 4 as an added service day
explain: exception_type 1 adds service on that date even though the weekly pattern says no. calendar_dates.txt modifies calendar.txt; that is exactly how special event or holiday services are added.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Why old attacks still matter: five eras, five patterns
question: A 2021 bug let text written into a log message be treated as an instruction by the logging library. Which 1960s problem has the same root pattern?
options: Phone phreaks guessing operator passwords
Mainframe users sharing accounts
Blue boxes: a caller's tone on the voice line was taken as a command by the switch
Stolen magnetic-stripe cards
explain: Both let data travelling on the normal channel (a sound on the voice line, text in a log message) act as control. The other options are real problems but different patterns: weak secrets, shared accounts and physical theft.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Melissa and ILOVEYOU: viruses that used your address book
question: Melissa sent itself to 50 contacts. Which control from the post-2000 Outlook changes most directly slows that kind of spread?
options: Asking the user before a program reads the address book, and a forced wait before each programmatic send
Encrypting the mailbox at rest
A longer password for Outlook
Disabling spell checking
explain: Melissa and ILOVEYOU used Outlook's programming interface to collect addresses and send mail. Prompts and delays on those actions break the automatic fan-out.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Target, Sony and OPM: breaches that reached boardrooms and governments
question: Why is the OPM fingerprint theft arguably worse than a card theft of similar size?
options: A card can be cancelled and reissued, but a fingerprint and the personal history in a clearance file cannot be changed
Fingerprints are worth more on criminal markets
Fingerprints were stored unencrypted
Card thefts are never reported
explain: Harm depends on what was taken, not only how many records. Card numbers are replaced routinely; biometrics and clearance histories are permanent and useful to an intelligence service for years.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: MOVEit and xz: mass extortion and the backdoor that almost shipped
question: What made the MOVEit campaign 'extortion without encryption'?
options: Cl0p encrypted files but did not ask for money
MOVEit encrypted the files itself
Victims paid before any data was taken
Cl0p stole data through the SQL injection and web shell and threatened to publish it, without encrypting victims' systems
explain: The advisory describes data theft through the LEMURLOOT web shell. The leverage was the threat of publication, so backups alone could not help.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: perf stat: counting, multiplexing and scaled estimates
question: A pinned event cannot get a counter. What does the perf_event_open man page say happens?
options: It goes into an error state and read returns end-of-file until it is re-enabled
It is multiplexed like any other event
The kernel evicts the NMI watchdog to make room
The count is silently reported as zero forever
explain: Pinned asks for the event to always be on the PMU. If that is impossible it does not fall back to multiplexing: it enters an error state where read(2) returns 0 bytes until it is disabled and enabled again.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Timing attacks on RSA: Kocher 1996 and remote timing in 2003
question: A team proposes adding a random 0 to 50 ms delay to every RSA operation instead of enabling blinding. What is the best response?
options: Accept: random delay makes timing attacks impossible
Accept, as long as the delay uses a cryptographic random generator
Reject, because delays are slower than blinding in every case
Reject: noise only multiplies the samples needed (roughly by the square of the noise), while blinding removes the attacker's knowledge of the input
explain: Kocher's analysis: samples needed grow with the square of the noise, so a patient attacker averages it away. Blinding breaks the link between the chosen input and what is exponentiated.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Spectre variant 1: speculating past a bounds check
question: In the Spectre v1 pattern, why is the secret byte multiplied by 4096 before indexing array2?
options: To encrypt it
Because pages must be accessed in order
To make the load slower and easier to time
So each possible value touches a different cache line and page, and the prefetcher does not pull in neighbours
explain: The covert channel needs one distinct, cleanly separated cache line per value. A 4096-byte stride puts each value on its own page, which also defeats prefetching across page boundaries.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Rowhammer: flipping bits in memory you never wrote
question: Why did the 2015 kernel exploit target page-table entries specifically?
options: One flipped bit in a PTE can redirect it to a page table the attacker controls, giving read-write access to all physical memory
Page tables are stored in the CPU cache, which is easier to hammer
PTEs are protected by ECC
The kernel rereads page tables every 64 ms
explain: A PTE holds a physical page number; flipping a low bit makes it point elsewhere. If it lands on one of the attacker's own page tables (memory was sprayed with them), the attacker can map any physical page.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Hardware supply chain, coordinated disclosure, and practice
question: Your company's code-signing tokens are found to contain an Infineon chip affected by ROCA. What is the necessary response?
options: Apply a firmware update; existing keys are then safe
Generate new keys on unaffected hardware and revoke the old public keys, because the existing keys can be factored from the public key alone
Nothing, because the tokens are FIPS 140-2 certified
Increase the RSA key length in the existing certificates
explain: ROCA's flaw is in how the primes were generated. Anyone with the public key can attempt the factorisation, so the keys themselves are weak: regenerate and revoke. Certification did not catch it. For long-lived signing keys, also plan the move to post-quantum signatures: NIST IR 8547 deprecates RSA after 2030.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: What a desync enables, and what defenders see
question: A front end logs 2 requests on upstream connection c9 and the back end logs 3. What is the most useful next step for a defender?
options: Ignore it; logs are often out of sync
Restart the browser
Inspect the extra back-end request and the client request that carried it, and check that tier's parser and desync settings
Rotate the TLS certificate
explain: A count mismatch on the same connection is the classic signature of a hidden request. The extra entry tells you what was smuggled; the client request before it tells you who sent it and which parsing gap was used.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: How HTTP caches decide: keys, freshness and Vary
question: Which response may a shared cache store, following RFC 9111?
options: 200 with Cache-Control: private
200 with Cache-Control: no-store
Any response to a request that carried an Authorization header, by default
200 with Cache-Control: max-age=600 and no other restrictions
explain: max-age gives explicit freshness and nothing forbids shared storage. private and no-store forbid it, and a request with Authorization may not be stored by a shared cache unless the response explicitly allows it.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: Path confusion at scale: delimiters, studies and ChatGPT 2023
question: In the USENIX 2020 study, what did the authors find about cache headers?
options: They always reveal whether a page was cached
They are forbidden by RFC 9111
Their presence was an unreliable indicator of whether a resource is cached, so tools relying on them can miss vulnerabilities
They prevent web cache deception
explain: The paper reports that the presence of cache headers was an unreliable indicator, implying that detection tools relying on that signal may produce false negatives.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Transparent Huge Pages: faults, khugepaged and memory bloat
question: A latency-critical service shows p99 spikes on allocation-heavy requests and a fast-rising compact_stall. THP is enabled=always, defrag=always. Which change targets the spikes while keeping most THP benefit?
options: Set defrag to defer so faults fall back to small pages and khugepaged collapses later
Set max_ptes_none to 0
Raise khugepaged pages_to_scan
Switch enabled to madvise and defrag to always
explain: The spikes come from direct compaction inside page faults. defer stops faults from stalling and leaves the work to kcompactd and khugepaged. max_ptes_none and pages_to_scan only affect khugepaged, not fault stalls, and madvise mode with defrag=always still stalls in any region the app marks.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: The SSM layer inside a hybrid: Mamba-2 as gated linear attention
question: During decoding at 100K tokens of context, which part of a Mamba-2 layer's per-sequence memory grows with the context?
options: The SSM state h
The convolution buffer
Both, linearly in context length
Neither; both have fixed size
explain: Both the state (heads x head dim x N) and the convolution window (4 inputs) are fixed by the architecture. That fixed size is exactly why hybrids use these layers, and also why they cannot store unlimited exact detail.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Serving a hybrid: prefix caching, rollback and chunked prefill
question: A hybrid's Mamba layer state is 1 MiB and one token of one attention layer's KV is 2 KiB. Under vLLM's rule that one attention block must hold at least one Mamba state's bytes, what is the smallest attention block size?
options: 16 tokens
256 tokens
512 tokens
1,024 tokens
explain: 1 MiB is 1,048,576 bytes; divided by 2,048 bytes per token that is 512 tokens. Blocks that large make prefix-cache hits coarse, which is why vLLM's design doc calls 400-plus-token blocks too large.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion: fusing by rank, not score
question: With k = 60, BM25 returns documents scoring 41.2 and 40.9 at ranks 1 and 2, and a second run with a different tokenizer returns 9.3 and 2.1 at ranks 1 and 2. How do the RRF contributions of these four positions compare?
options: The first run contributes far more because its scores are larger
Rank 1 gets 1/61 and rank 2 gets 1/62 in both runs; raw score gaps are ignored
The second run contributes more because its gap between ranks is bigger
They cannot be compared without normalizing first
explain: RRF uses only positions. That makes it immune to score scales (good) but blind to the fact that the second run is much more confident about its top hit (information lost). Bruch et al. argue this loss of score information is one reason a tuned convex combination can beat RRF.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: When fusion hurts, and weighting per query
question: Support search fuses BM25 (standard analyzer) and dense vectors with one alpha of 0.7 toward dense. Users typing part numbers like XJ47B, without the hyphen used in the catalog, get poor results. What fixes it?
options: Raise alpha to 1.0 so the embedding handles part numbers
Lower RRF's k so the top BM25 hit counts more
Index a codes subfield that removes hyphens before tokenizing, and route code-like queries to a lexical-heavy weight that includes that field
Switch to z-score normalization
explain: Neither weight nor normalization helps while the lexical side cannot match: XJ47B is one token and the index holds xj and 47b. Fix the analysis so both spellings produce xj47b, then give identifier queries a lexical-heavy weight, since an embedding blurs nearby codes.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Latency, cost, and when HyDE hurts
question: A support search box must answer in 300 ms at p99 (the 99th percentile: 99 of every 100 requests must finish within 300 ms). Which HyDE plan is realistic?
options: HyDE with N=8 sequential calls
HyDE with N=8 parallel samples
Do not run HyDE on the request path; use it offline or only for a slow fallback path, and serve plain or hybrid retrieval online
Keep HyDE but drop the embedding step
explain: Even one generation is seconds in the measurements cited (over 2000 ms in query2doc, 11.58 s per query in the RAG study). Parallel sampling bounds wall time to one generation, which still breaks 300 ms. HyDE fits batch or asynchronous paths, not this budget.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: How a PLC thinks: the scan cycle and ladder logic
question: A PLC reads inputs into an image table at the start of each scan. If an attacker could change the input image after it is read but before the logic runs, what would the logic do?
options: Detect the change and fault
Act on the false values as if they were real measurements
Ignore the input image and read sensors directly
Stop scanning
explain: MITRE describes the image table as what the user program uses 'instead of directly interacting with physical I/O'. Manipulating it makes correct logic act on false inputs, the essence of Stuxnet's design.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: How attacks on physical processes work
question: Why did the replay in the scenario defeat the operator but not the safety system?
options: The safety system ignores sensors
Safety systems cannot be attacked
The replay was too slow
The SIS used its own sensor and logic, which were not on the path the attacker manipulated
explain: The replay changed what the HMI displayed. The SIS read the real level through its own transmitter and acted independently. Triton (lesson 11) shows attackers going after that last layer too, which is why its independence matters so much.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: IT/OT convergence: Colonial, Oldsmar, Unitronics, Volt Typhoon
question: Colonial's OT was not shown to be infected, yet the pipeline stopped for five days. What design lesson does CISA's advisory AA21-131A draw?
options: OT should share IT's ransomware backups
Move OT to the cloud
Pay ransoms faster
Ensure the OT network can operate at necessary capacity even if the IT network is compromised, with robust IT/OT segmentation and tested manual controls
explain: CISA and FBI urged that OT be able to keep running when IT is compromised, plus segmentation, a DMZ and regularly tested manual controls. Dependence on IT systems, not OT damage, drove the outage.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Rules and maps: NERC CIP, IEC 62443, NIST, CISA and ATT&CK for ICS
question: An intruder raises the high-level alarm threshold on the HMI so operators are never warned. Which ATT&CK for ICS tactic is this?
options: Collection
Discovery
Inhibit Response Function
Command and Control
explain: MITRE: in Inhibit Response Function 'the adversary is trying to prevent your safety, protection, quality assurance, and operator intervention functions from responding'. Modify Alarm Settings and Alarm Suppression are techniques under it.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: SAML web SSO step by step: AuthnRequest, bindings and RelayState
question: A security review finds an SP that redirects to whatever URL arrives in RelayState after login. What is the risk?
options: None: RelayState is signed by the IdP
An open redirect: attackers can send users through a real login and then on to a phishing page
The assertion will expire
The IdP will refuse to log the user in
explain: RelayState is not covered by the assertion's signature and returns through the browser. OWASP's advice is to validate it against an allowlist when it carries a URL.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: OIDC as the modern alternative: the same job in JSON
question: Which SAML check corresponds to an OIDC relying party comparing the ID token's nonce with the value it stored before redirecting?
options: Checking AudienceRestriction
Checking InResponseTo against an AuthnRequest this session sent
Checking the Issuer
Checking SessionNotOnOrAfter
explain: Both bind the statement to a login request that this browser session started, which stops an attacker injecting a response or ID token obtained elsewhere.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Conditional access: deciding at sign-in, and what happens after
question: Two Conditional Access policies apply to a sign-in: one requires MFA and one requires a compliant device. What does Entra require?
options: Either MFA or a compliant device
Both MFA and a compliant device
Only the newer policy
Only the stricter policy
explain: Microsoft's documentation: when multiple policies apply, all applicable policies must be satisfied, so the user needs MFA and a compliant device.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: The federation defender's checklist, and where to practise
question: During a suspected Golden SAML incident, which response step must come first?
options: Rotate the token-signing certificate
Regain administrative control of the IdP from clean machines and remove the attacker's access
Reset all user passwords
Disable SCIM
explain: Microsoft and CISA both stress that rotating keys while the attacker still controls the IdP only hands them the new key. Control first, then rotate twice, update relying parties and revoke tokens.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Access reviews and certification: asking again, and meaning it
question: A quarterly review of the admin console finishes 100% complete. One reviewer approved 212 of 212 items in about 2 seconds each. What should happen next?
options: Nothing: the campaign completed on time
Delete the reviewer's own account
Treat those decisions as unreviewed: re-run them with usage context or a different reviewer, and follow up with the reviewer
Approve all items automatically next quarter to save time
explain: Completion is not quality. Uniform approval at two seconds an item suggests nobody judged the need, so the decisions provide no assurance. Re-review with context, and treat reviewer behaviour as a metric.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: PAM vaults: check-out, rotation, and the Uber 2022 script
question: After the Uber pattern, a team moves the PAM admin password from a script into an environment variable on the same file server. What is still wrong?
options: Nothing: environment variables are encrypted
PowerShell cannot read environment variables
The password is now too short
A static PAM admin secret is still stored where people and processes on that server can read it, and the job still runs with vault admin rights
explain: Moving a static secret to another readable place does not satisfy IA-5(7)'s intent, and the job still holds far more privilege than reporting needs. Remove the secret and the excess privilege.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Service accounts and non-human identities
question: An engineer logs in interactively with the deployment service account because their own account lacks production rights. Which OWASP NHI risk is this, and why does it matter?
options: NHI10 Human Use of NHI: actions can no longer be tied to a person, and it bypasses the controls on the engineer's own account
NHI3 Vulnerable Third-Party NHI: the vendor is at fault
NHI6 Insecure Cloud Deployment Configurations: the cloud is misconfigured
It is not a risk if the password is strong
explain: Using a machine identity as a person breaks accountability and sidesteps the approval, MFA and review that apply to the engineer's own access.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Differencing and picking a threshold with Otsu's method
question: Applying Otsu to the difference of two aligned photos where nothing changed (only sensor noise), what do you expect?
options: An empty mask, because Otsu detects that there is only one class
An error from OpenCV
A mask flagging a sizable fraction of noise pixels
A mask with exactly one pixel
explain: Otsu has no notion of 'one class'. It maximizes between-class variance over all splits, which always exists, so it will cut the noise distribution somewhere near its middle. Guard against this with a minimum threshold or a test on the gap between class means.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: The IR lifecycle: NIST 800-61r3, CSF 2.0 and SANS PICERL
question: In the SANS PICERL model, why does containment include a "system back-up" step before long-term containment?
options: To restore the user's files faster
To take a forensic image of affected systems before they are wiped or rebuilt, preserving evidence
Because backups are required before any patch
To test the backup software
explain: The handbook places a forensic image (it names commercial forensic imaging tools such as FTK (Forensic Toolkit) and EnCase) before wiping and reimaging, so the evidence survives for prosecution or for the lessons-learned analysis.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Evidence first: the order of volatility (RFC 3227)
question: RFC 3227 asks you to record the difference between the system clock and UTC. Why?
options: To meet a legal formatting rule
Because UTC is more secure
To detect whether the attacker changed the time zone
So that timestamps from this system can be aligned with other sources when building a timeline
explain: Timelines merge events from many machines. A server whose clock is 4 minutes fast puts its events in the wrong order relative to the firewall unless you record and correct the drift.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Linux artefacts: shell history, auth logs, cron, systemd, timestamps
question: A compromised server's /root/.bash_history has no commands from the intrusion window. Which conclusion is justified?
options: The attacker never used a root shell
Nothing: history is written at shell exit, can be disabled or redirected, and may never have been saved
The history file must have been edited
Root logins are not recorded by Linux
explain: Missing history is an absence of evidence, not evidence of absence. Look for other sources: auth logs, the journal, process accounting if enabled, file timestamps, and memory.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Ransomware response: pay or not, law enforcement and sanctions
question: During the 2017 NotPetya outbreak, a victim pays the ransom. What happens, according to Kaspersky's analysis?
options: They get a working key within hours
Nothing useful: the installation ID was random, so the attackers had no way to produce a key for that disk
Only the master boot record is restored
The payment is automatically refunded
explain: Kaspersky found the installation ID that a real ransomware operator needs for key recovery was generated from random data. NotPetya was a wiper presented as ransomware.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: When data becomes code: the one idea behind every injection
question: A program reads a city name and runs `eval("lookup('" + city + "')")`. A user types `Paris`. Another types `x') or delete_all('`. What does the second input do?
options: Nothing, because the city name is inside quotes
Python raises an error because quotes are not allowed in strings
It closes the quoted string early and adds a second function call to the expression
It only looks up a city literally named with those characters
explain: The built string becomes lookup('x') or delete_all(''). (Python's or runs delete_all only if lookup('x') returns a false value; an attacker would pick an operator that always runs the second call, but either way it is code the programmer never wrote.) The first quote in the input closes the string literal the programmer opened, so the rest is parsed as code. Quotes only protect data if the data cannot contain the closing quote.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Heartland and TalkTalk: SQL injection as the way in
question: The ICO found that TalkTalk's vulnerable pages came from Tiscali, which it had acquired years earlier. Which control most directly addresses that root cause?
options: A longer password policy for staff
Encrypting backups
An inventory of every web application you expose, including acquired ones, with owners who patch and test them
Moving the database to a different vendor
explain: The pages were vulnerable, unpatched and apparently unknown to the people responsible. Knowing what you run, and giving each system an owner, is the precondition for fixing it.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: MOVEit 2023: one SQL injection, thousands of victims
question: You patched MOVEit on 3 June 2023. What should you do next?
options: Nothing: the patch removes the vulnerability and any damage
Rotate the TLS certificate
Hunt for signs of earlier compromise, such as human2.aspx files, "Health Check Service" accounts and unusual requests in web logs
Switch the database engine
explain: Exploitation began on 27 May, before any patch existed. A web shell installed before patching keeps working afterwards, so you must look for persistence and data theft, then remove and report them.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Server-side template injection
question:
Which change fixes `render_template_string("

" + request.args["title"] + "

")` in a Flask (Python web framework) app?
options: Turn on autoescape
Strip the characters { and } from title

Use a constant template and pass title as a variable: render_template_string("

{{ title }}

", title=request.args["title"])
Use HTTPS
explain: The fix moves the input from template source to template data. Autoescape only affects output encoding, and stripping braces is a denylist that may miss other syntax such as {% %} or engine-specific forms.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Two shared rings: SQEs, CQEs, head and tail
question: A 4-entry SQ has tail counter 9. Which slot does the next SQE go into?
options: Slot 1, because 9 & 3 = 1
Slot 9, the tail value
Slot 0, because the ring is full after 4
Slot 2, because the next SQE goes one past the tail: 10 & 3 = 2
explain: The slot is `tail & (entries - 1)` = 9 & 3 = 1. The tail counter itself is never reset; it just keeps counting and the mask wraps it onto the 4 slots.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Inside a connected device: microcontrollers, flash and the boot ROM
question: Why are lock flags such as 'debugging disabled' stored in OTP bits rather than in flash?
options: An OTP bit, once set, cannot be cleared by software that later gains control
OTP is faster to read at boot
Flash cannot store single bits
OTP is encrypted automatically
explain: The point of a lock is that nobody can undo it later, including malicious code. OTP bits only change one way. A flag in flash could be rewritten by anyone who can write flash. Speed and encryption are not the reason.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Secure boot: a chain of trust that starts in ROM
question: A bootloader computes SHA-256 of the application and compares it with a hash stored next to the application in flash. What does this protect against?
options: An attacker who can write flash replacing the application
Accidental corruption of the application, but not deliberate replacement
Both corruption and replacement
Neither
explain: Whoever can write the new application can also write its new hash, so a bare hash only detects accidents. A signature checked against a key fingerprint the attacker cannot change (in OTP) is what stops deliberate replacement.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: A/B slots, trial boots and recovery from a bad update
question: A camera is on trial with firmware 4.0 (PENDING_VERIFY) when the power fails. What does ESP-IDF's bootloader do on the next start, with rollback enabled?
options: Boots 4.0 again and waits for confirmation
Erases both slots
Boots the factory image and burns the anti-rollback fuse
Marks 4.0 ABORTED and boots the previous valid image
explain: An image that reboots while still PENDING_VERIFY was never confirmed. ESP-IDF marks it aborted and returns to the last valid application. Nothing is erased, and the security version is only raised after a successful confirmation.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Device vulnerability handling: disclosure, SBOMs and the CRA
question: Under the CRA, which deadline applies to a manufacturer's first notification of an actively exploited vulnerability?
options: 24 hours for an early warning
72 hours
14 days
One month
explain: The early warning is due within 24 hours, the main notification within 72 hours, and the final report no later than 14 days after a fix or mitigation is available. One month is the final-report deadline for severe incidents.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Prototype pollution: one request changes every object
question: A code reviewer sees `target[k1][k2] = v` where `k1` and `k2` come from a JSON body. The team proposes rejecting only the key `__proto__`. What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing: __proto__ is the only way to reach Object.prototype
k1 = constructor and a deeper write via prototype still reach Object.prototype; refuse all three names or use own-key checks and null-prototype objects
JSON.parse already removes __proto__, so the check is redundant
The check must be case-insensitive because JavaScript property names ignore case
explain: MDN describes the constructor.prototype route explicitly, and our test showed it working even with --disable-proto=delete. JSON.parse keeps __proto__ as an own key rather than removing it, and property names are case-sensitive.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: ReDoS: a regular expression that blocks every user
question: Why is a 2-second regex match worse on a Node.js server than on a server that runs each request on its own thread?
options: Because V8 cannot run regular expressions on a worker thread
Because Node.js restarts the process whenever a regex exceeds one second
It is not worse: Node.js automatically moves regexes to the Worker Pool
Because Node.js runs every request's JavaScript on one Event Loop, so the match delays all other clients, not just the attacker
explain: Regex matching is ordinary JavaScript work on the Event Loop. The Worker Pool runs only specific I/O and CPU APIs. A thread-per-request server would lose one thread; a Node.js process loses all its JavaScript capacity for the duration.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Deserialisation in JavaScript: node-serialize to React2Shell
question: A team wants to send a 'job' object containing a callback function from one service to another and proposes node-serialize. What should they do instead?
options: Use node-serialize but strip the function marker with a regex
Use eval on the receiving side but inside a try/catch
Base64-encode the serialised object so it cannot be tampered with
Send only data (for example a job type name and JSON parameters), validate it with a schema, and map the type name to code the receiving service already contains
explain: Code should never travel as data across a trust boundary. An allowlist of job types mapped to local functions gives the same flexibility with no deserialisation of code. Regex stripping is a blocklist, try/catch does not stop code from running, and Base64 is an encoding, not protection.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Electron: when XSS in a desktop app becomes code execution
question: Which single change would have broken the Discord chain at the navigation step?
options: Raising the bug bounty
Turning nodeIntegration on
Adding the sandbox attribute to the embed iframes, so they cannot navigate the top-level window
Loading the embed over HTTP instead of HTTPS
explain: Both Discord's interim fix and Electron's advisory workaround were to sandbox iframes. Without the top-level navigation, the iframe's XSS stays inside the iframe, which has no access to the main window's built-ins or preload API.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: mimalloc: three free lists per page
question: A loop does `p = malloc(48); free(p);` a billion times on one thread. Without `local_free` (frees pushed straight onto `free`), what would mimalloc lose?
options: The guarantee that the slow path runs regularly, so remote frees and deferred work could wait forever
Correctness: blocks would be handed out twice
Locality, because blocks would come from other pages
Nothing; local_free exists only for debugging
explain: With one list, the same block is pushed and popped forever and free never empties, so malloc_generic never runs. thread_free would never be collected and deferred-free callbacks would never fire. local_free makes free run dry after a bounded number of allocations.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Histories: invoke, ok, fail, and the indeterminate info
question: A test with 5 client processes runs for 10 minutes and 40 writes end as info. Roughly how many operations can be concurrent near the end of the history?
options: At most 5, because there are only 5 processes
Exactly 40, the info writes alone
Zero, because the test is over
Up to about 45: the 5 live processes plus 40 writes that might still take effect
explain: Each info write stays open until the end of the history, and the crashed processes were replaced by fresh ones that keep issuing operations. So concurrency near the end is the live processes plus every unresolved info op, which is what makes checking expensive.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: The knobs, and how fast the space grows
question: You add one more knob to the matmul kernel: a vector width with 3 legal values. Everything else is unchanged. What happens to the 6000-configuration space?
options: It grows by 3 configurations, to 6003
It triples, to 18000 configurations
It stays at 6000 because vector width is derived from BLOCK_K
It grows only if you also add shapes to the key
explain: Knobs combine multiplicatively: every existing configuration is now three configurations, one per vector width. This is why autotuning is a search problem rather than a loop over a list, and why pruning matters before you compile anything.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The per-packet budget: why the kernel path runs out of cycles
question: Why do people benchmark packet I/O with 64 byte frames rather than 1500 byte frames?
options: Because they maximize packets per second, so fixed per-packet costs (interrupts, syscalls, metadata) dominate and are exposed
Because 64 byte frames are the most common size on real networks
Because NICs can only DMA 64 bytes at a time
Because larger frames do not fit in a 2 KiB packet buffer
explain: Throughput in bits is the same, but small frames mean the most packets per second, and most driver and stack costs are per packet, not per byte. That is the worst case a data plane must survive.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Worked example: how SPDK reaches 10 million IOPS on one thread
question: With SPDK's deferred-doorbell option on, a thread calls spdk_nvme_ns_cmd_read 16 times and then calls spdk_nvme_qpair_process_completions once. How many SQ tail doorbell writes did those 16 submissions need?
options: 0, NVMe needs no doorbell
explain: With the option set, submission only builds commands in the SQ ring; the doorbell is rung inside the poll call, once for everything submitted since the last poll.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: Driver signing: from cross-signing to Microsoft's portal
question: A vendor wants a new kernel driver to reach retail users through Windows Update on Windows 11 and Windows Server 2025. Which signing route fits?
options: HLK testing and WHCP (dashboard) signing
Attestation signing with an EV certificate
Cross-signing with a commercial CA certificate
Test signing with the TESTSIGNING boot option
explain: Attestation-signed drivers cannot be published to Windows Update for retail audiences and do not load on Windows Server 2016 and later. Cross-signing is no longer accepted, and test signing is for development machines. HLK-tested WHCP signing covers client and Server.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: Buffers, double fetches and Microsoft's driver security checklist
question: Which checklist item most directly reduces the chance that an overclocking utility's driver becomes a BYOVD tool on PCs from other manufacturers?
options: Restrict software-only drivers to the hardware they serve, for example by checking SMBIOS before enabling capabilities
Add SAL annotations
Use NonPagedPoolNx for allocations
Run BinSkim before release
explain: Software-only drivers can be loaded on any PC, which is what makes them portable attack tools. Microsoft's checklist says they must verify they run on the intended hardware, using a unique PnP (Plug and Play) ID or an SMBIOS check. The other items improve quality but do not limit where the driver works.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: App Control driver policies: allow what you run, deny what you know
question: Your allowlist trusts Fabrikam drivers at WHQLPublisher level. Microsoft's blocklist, deployed as a second policy, denies Fabrikam toyfan.sys up to 1.4. Will ToyFan 1.3 load?
options: No, because a file must pass every active policy and explicit deny rules are processed first
Yes, because the allow rule names the publisher
Yes, because the blocklist contains Allow All rules
It depends on the order the policies were deployed
explain: With multiple policies, a file must be allowed by each of them. The blocklist policy denies ToyFan 1.3; its Allow All rules only mean it does not restrict anything else. Within any one policy, explicit deny rules take precedence over allow rules.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: Responding to a BYOVD alert, and the cost of kernel code
question: After removing a malicious driver's service and file, and updating the blocklist, why is a reboot part of eradication?
options: To rotate the BitLocker key
Because a driver that is already loaded stays in kernel memory until restart; removing the file and adding blocks does not unload it
Because Sysmon only logs after a reboot
Because the blocklist only works in Safe Mode
explain: Microsoft's blocklist page notes that already running drivers the policy would block keep running until the computer restarts. Deleting the file does not unmap the code from kernel memory either.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Limits of fusion and how compilers decide
question: In the PyTorch 2 ablation, disabling both fusion and inlining made compiled models slower than eager. Why?
options: torch.compile adds Python overhead per op
Inductor decomposes large operators into many primitives and relies on fusion to recombine them
Triton kernels are slower than CUDA kernels
Graph breaks increase without fusion
explain: The paper explains that decompositions break large optimized operators into smaller primitive ops, and fusion recombines them. Without fusion and inlining each primitive becomes its own kernel with its own HBM round trip, so the result is slower than eager's hand-written kernels.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: The distillation loss and why it is scaled by T squared
question: Your transfer set is 2 million unlabeled product photos plus 5,000 labeled ones. What is a sensible way to set alpha?
options: alpha = 0, since human labels are more reliable than any teacher
alpha = 0.5 everywhere, so neither term dominates
Copy the PyTorch tutorial's 0.25 soft and 0.75 hard weights
alpha = 1 (pure distillation) on the unlabeled photos, and tune alpha jointly with T on held-out data for the labeled ones
explain: Unlabeled examples have no hard-label term, so only the soft loss applies to them. Where labels exist, the right mix is an empirical question: Hinton et al. found a low hard-label weight best, the tutorial uses the opposite, and T shifts the balance, so tune T and alpha together on held-out data.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: An LLM distillation pipeline: logits, tokenizers, traces, compute
question: You stored each position's top-64 teacher entries and renormalized them to sum to 1. Compared with full-distribution distillation, what should you expect, and what is the cheapest mitigation Busbridge et al. found?
options: A student that is too confident on the kept tokens; mix in cross-entropy on the real next tokens
A student that is too uncertain; raise the temperature
No effect, since the dropped tokens carry almost no probability
A student whose vocabulary shrinks to 64 tokens; store the full distribution instead
explain: Renormalizing assigns zero to every token outside the top k, so the target is sharper than the teacher and even a perfect copy of the teacher is penalized (0.223 nats in the toy). In their study top-128 cost 0.11 nats, and a 0.7 distillation plus 0.3 next-token mix recovered it to within 0.01 nats.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sharing keys and values across heads: MQA and GQA
question: In GQA with 32 query heads and 8 KV heads, what does each KV head serve?
options: A group of 4 query heads
One query head; the other 24 are unused
All 32 query heads
8 consecutive tokens
explain: Query heads are split into 8 groups of 4, and each group shares one key head and one value head.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters
question: Which statement about H2O is correct?
options: It needs the model to be fine-tuned
It scores tokens by attention they received in past steps, as a proxy for future importance
It keeps every token but at lower precision
It keeps only heavy hitters and no recent tokens
explain: H2O is training-free and uses local statistics: the sum of attention each token received so far. The paper finds this as effective as using future attention, and that keeping both heavy hitters and recent tokens is needed.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Build and test it: quantize real keys, then evict on a needle test
question: You deploy SnapKV for a RAG service and accuracy is poor on facts buried in the documents. Your harness shows that compression runs before the user's question is appended, with a 64-token observation window. What is the most direct fix?
options: Switch to StreamingLLM
Lower compression_ratio to 0.1 and keep the 64-token window
Compress after the question is in the prompt, with an observation window about the question's length
Quantize the cache to FP8 instead
explain: In the lab's run (50 trials per setting), SnapKV without the question scored 0% at every ratio, and a 64-query window diluted by filler reached at most 28%; a 16-query window over the question reached 98% to 100% even at 75% removed. StreamingLLM drops old documents by position, and FP8 does not reduce the token count.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, capacity and reuse
lessonTitle: Finding a prefix across tiers, requests and engines
question: A request's blocks are h0 to h9. HBM holds h0 to h3. The CPU tier holds h0 to h6 and h8, h9. What gets loaded from CPU, and what is recomputed?
options: Load h4 to h6 and h8, h9; recompute h7
Load h4 to h6; recompute h7, h8, h9
Load nothing; recompute h4 to h9, since the CPU tier has a gap
Load h0 to h6 again from CPU to refresh them; recompute h7 to h9
explain: The usable prefix stops at the first block that is nowhere: h7. h4 to h6 extend the GPU hit contiguously, so they are loaded. h8 and h9 were computed after a context that includes h7, which must be recomputed, so they are recomputed along with it.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, capacity and reuse
lessonTitle: Hands-on: configure an offload tier and measure it
question: A GPU holds 40 GB of KV cache. You enable vLLM's OffloadingConnector with `cpu_bytes_to_use` set to 30 GB. How many extra hits should the CPU tier add?
options: About 75% more, since 30 GB is 75% of HBM
Twice as many, since the cache doubles in size
It depends only on the eviction policy
Almost none: blocks are copied out as soon as they are computed, so a tier smaller than HBM only mirrors blocks HBM still holds
explain: Offloading is immediate, so the CPU tier holds copies of recent blocks, most of which are still in HBM. Only a tier larger than the aggregate GPU KV cache keeps blocks HBM has already evicted. vLLM's tuning guide says exactly this.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Hybrid logical clocks: Lamport order that stays near real time
question: A node at (10, 3) receives a message stamped (8, 7) when its physical clock reads 9. What is the result?
explain: l = max(10, 8, 9) = 10 equals only the old l, so c = 3 + 1 = 4, giving (10, 4). The message's counter 7 is ignored because its l is smaller: (8, 7) is already less than (10, 3). Taking max(c, cm) + 1 here would be a bug that inflates c.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Inside the encoders: markers, [MASK] padding and training
question: ColBERTv2 distills a cross-encoder with a KL-divergence loss over a 64-way score distribution instead of regressing the cross-encoder's raw scores with mean squared error. What is the reason the paper gives?
options: KL divergence is cheaper to compute than MSE
ColBERT's scores (sums of cosines) have a restricted scale that may not line up with the cross-encoder's output scale; KL compares the distributions over passages instead
MSE cannot be backpropagated through a max operation
The cross-encoder only outputs binary labels
explain: A sum of 32 cosines lives in a fixed range, while a cross-encoder's logits can be on any scale. Matching softmax distributions over the same 64 passages only asks ColBERT to rank them the same way, which is what retrieval needs.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why reasoning in word tokens is a bottleneck
question: Why does writing reasoning tokens let a fixed-depth transformer solve problems it cannot solve in one pass?
options: Generated tokens are fed back as inputs, so later passes can build on earlier results, increasing effective serial depth
Longer outputs give the attention softmax a sharper distribution
Each written token adds new trainable parameters at inference
The KV cache stores the answer before it is written
explain: Each pass has bounded depth L. Feeding outputs back chains passes together, so n written steps allow roughly n x L layers of sequential computation. Coconut keeps this feedback loop but passes a vector instead of a token.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why superposition works: continuous thoughts and graph reachability
question: In the 7-node example, why does G never appear in any thought?
options: Its weight is filtered out by the MLP for being too small
No edge leads into G, so it is not reachable; the edge G to D is only attended when G is already in the set
G is a candidate, and candidates are excluded from thoughts
G appears in t3 but is cancelled by layer normalization
explain: Layer 2 attends to edges by their source. G's only edge leaves G, and G is never reachable from A, so that edge never matches and nothing adds G. The final measurement then reads 0 for G and 0.408 for F.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: An index is a model: predicting where a key sits
